newsitem.title: CHINA: Big Asia smoking nations cool on U.S. tobacco pact.
newsitem.headline: Big Asia smoking nations cool on U.S. tobacco pact.

text.p: Asia's cigarette lords were undaunted on Monday by a landmark pact under which U.S. tobacco firms admit the leaf is addictive, confident in strong domestic markets that in many cases are protected from foreign imports.

In China, the world's biggest cigarette market, officials shrugged off last Friday's U.S. settlement under which tobacco companies agreed to pay $368.5 billion, admit that tobacco is addictive and accept extensive federal regulation over their products and advertising. "This cannot affect China's market," said an official of the State Tobacco Monopoly.
"They (foreign firms) often have new policies, but it cannot directly influence China," he said. "We have our own methods."
Industry experts saw scant chance despite increasing numbers of smokers in much of Asia for U.S. tobacco firms wanting to offset damage to domestic sales by boosting marketing abroad.
Tariffs of 150 percent in China acted as an effective barrier to foreign brands reaching its 300 million smokers.

Smokers in China are increasing, their numbers growing by 2.0 percent a year compared with developed world rates where smokers are falling by about 1.0 percent, but most are loyal to -- and can only afford -- domestic brands.
Foreign brands account for less than 10 percent of China's sales of 1.6 trillion cigarettes a year -- and monopoly officials say almost every foreign cigarette is smuggled.
"The impact of foreign tobacco companies in China is not big," acknowledged a Shanghai-based official of B.A.T Industries Plc.
With cigarettes the biggest single source of state revenue -- one-eighth of the annual total -- the government has little incentive to penalise the industry to save on health costs.
"Tobacco firms in China are state-owned so they would be taking with one hand and giving with the other," said business consultant and industry expert Peter Batey.
A few cosmetic gestures have resulted in a ban -- widely ignored -- on smoking in public places. Limits on advertising in sport have prompted cigarette firms to opt to sponsor instead.
Japan, another country with a large contingent of heavy smokers headed by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, also depends heavily on tobacco revenues.

The powerful Finance Ministry controls the tobacco industry and enjoys a hefty revenue from a cigarette sales. It announced this month that while tax revenue from liquor sales edged down 0.3 percent to 130,203 million yen from last year, revenue from tobacco had soared 35.0 percent to 113,683 million yen. "The United States is a litigious society (unlike Japan), and I don't think the settlement would have any immediate impact on Japan's tobacco industry," said Masako Nagayasu, analyst at Kankaku Research Institute Corp.
"The demand for cigarettes is in itself on a declining trend," she said. Industry officials in India, the third largest producer of tobacco, were reluctant to comment on the U.S. pact.

Even India's 200 million smokers may not be the answer for U.S. manufacturers seeking alternative markets. Only 25 percent smoke cigarettes. The rest prefer cigars, cheroots, bidis -- crushed tobacco rolled in a dried tobacco leaf -- or just chew the leaf.

Singapore has already declared war on tobacco, enforcing a ban in government buildings, restaurants, department stores, air-conditioned offices, factory floors, lifts, taxis and buses, and the 55,000-seat open-air National Stadium. Hong Kong toughened its anti-smoking law in 1994, requiring all tobacco products to display health warnings and banning advertising on television.
The legislature debates a new smoking bill next week that proposes a total ban on advertising and higher fines.
Indonesia may offer better prospects.
PT BAT, which dominates the market for foreign brands, predicts at least five percent growth a year in cigarette sales in a country of 200 million people where most men smoke.
Although most Indonesians prefer the local clove-flavoured "kretek" cigarettes, foreign brands are making rapid inroads.
As in China and Japan, hefty tax revenues may deter the government from drastic action against the industry.
New Zealand is one market that has been contracting, by about 2.0 percent a year for the last 30 years.

The U.S. settlement could have implications for future anti-smoking laws in New Zealand, Associate Health Minister Neil Kirton said. "Obviously the settlement has major implications for anti-tobacco legislation on an international scale," Kirton said. "The proposed regulations will set a benchmark against which other anti-smoking measures will need to be judged."
